title: In 3 adult fly connectomes, homologous synapse counts vary as 2 to 3 times Poisson plus a 0.2 to 0.3 log-SD edge term after neuron gains; T-bars and clusters to 4 µm do not explain the 2 to 3 factor
abstract: Question: a prior SCI study found that two copies of the same adult fly connection vary more than Poisson sampling, and that the excess increases with the synapse count. What is this excess, and at which anatomical level is it set? Approach: we used the exact conditional binomial test on cell types with one neuron per side in FlyWire v783 (left versus right), male CNS v1.0 (left versus right) and FlyWire versus hemibrain v1.2 (two animals). We compared one global scale, neuron gains, neuron x neuropil gains and measured neuropil totals, all evaluated on held-out connections with held-out Poisson nulls. We split the held-out excess into a constant factor kappa and an edge-specific SD sigma of log(muA/muB), from E[r^2] = kappa + sigma^2 n p(1-p). Results: kappa was 2.0 to 3.0 in all comparisons and almost no normalisation changed it. Neuron gains reduced sigma (excess over null) from 0.58 to 0.27-0.29 between FlyWire and the hemibrain, from 0.31 to 0.20 in FlyWire and from 0.28 to 0.21 in the male CNS. Neuron x neuropil gains gave in-sample phi near 2 but held-out phi of 3.2 to 3.8 (null 1.2 to 1.4), so in-sample values overstate them. In the male CNS, a T-bar almost never contacts the same partner twice (48,472,411 T-bar-partner pairs among 48,473,057 PSDs). Counting occupied 0.5 to 4 um grid cells lowered kappa from 2.94 to 1.55, but a saturation null with the real spatial clusters fell in the same way; the observed/null ratio stayed 2.6 to 2.9. kappa and sigma from one comparison gave 82 to 93% coverage of nominal 90% intervals for strong connections in another comparison, against 52 to 70% for Poisson. Limitations: between-animal comparisons confound animal and reconstruction pipeline; hemibrain neurons are truncated; only one-per-side cell types; the variance model is first order; the cause of kappa remains unknown.
